title: Y-R-A
hook: yirah means both fear and awe

segments.voice: Yesterday, L-M-D: talmid, Talmud, one root for learning and teaching. Your line was learning and teaching. Did you teach your sentence to someone? What did they add? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-one.

Jacob is running from his brother. Night falls on the road, and he lies down with a stone under his head. He dreams of a ladder set on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, and angels going up and down on it. Then he wakes on the same hard ground and says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." And the very next words: "And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place!" Afraid. Dreadful. Two English words, and in the Hebrew, both come from today's three letters.
screen: `A STONE FOR A PILLOW.` → `A LADDER IN A DREAM.` → `HOW DREADFUL IS THIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Y-R-A. Yod, resh, alef. Yirah: fear, and awe. Four scenes. First, Jacob. He was afraid, vayira, and the place was dreadful, nora. Jacob doesn't flee this place. He's shaken by it. He calls it "none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Second, wisdom. A psalm says: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Some readers hear yirah there less as terror and more as the right kind of smallness: knowing the world is bigger than you, and that you are not the center of it. Third, fear beside trust. At the sea, after the crossing, Exodus says: "and the people feared the LORD, and believed the LORD, and his servant Moses." Believed is a form of A-M-N, the root of steadiness from earlier this block. Here fear and faith stand side by side, not against each other. Fourth, how awe begins. Maimonides, in his Mishneh Torah, writes that when a person looks closely at the great and wondrous works of creation, love rises first, a longing to know. And right after, the person draws back, aware of how small and brief they are. That's yirah: fear that stays to look. The days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur are called the Yamim Noraim, the Days of Awe, from the same root as Jacob's dreadful place.
screen: `HOW DREADFUL IS THIS PLACE.` · `THE BEGINNING OF WISDOM.` · `FEARED, AND BELIEVED.` · `LOVE, THEN DRAWING BACK.` · then, large: `AWE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: awe at one thing. Settle, and breathe. Choose something close by and look at it closely, as if for the first time. Your own hand: the lines, the joints, the fact that it moves when you ask it to. Or the sky through a window. Or your breath, coming in without being called. Stay with it until it gets a little strange, a little large. Let yourself be small next to it. No need to explain it. If you pray, you can say Jacob's words: surely the LORD is in this place. The bell holds the time.
Y-R-A. Yod, resh, alef: fear and awe in one root. Jacob's dreadful place, and the Days of Awe. Today's word.
Your line: awe. Today, stop once in front of something ordinary, a tree, a face, a meal, and look until it becomes a little wondrous. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: The days from Rosh Hashanah through Yom Kippur are called the Days of Awe, and Jewish prayer books carry blessings for moments of wonder, such as seeing lightning or a great sea.

match.prompt: fear and awe — tap the pairs.

myth: the same root carries awe: Jacob's 'dreadful' place is the house of God.
at the sea, the people feared the LORD and believed
Exodus puts fear and faith side by side.
for Maimonides, awe comes with no love at all
he describes love rising first, then a drawing back in awe.

fork.setup: you're Jacob. you've woken on the road from a dream of a ladder to heaven, shaken. it's morning. what do you do?
options: leave quickly and never speak of it.
set up your stone pillow as a pillar and name the place.
lie down again to try to dream it twice.
fork.reveal: Jacob sets up the stone as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel, house of God. awe made him mark the spot.

original.note: Hebrew: fear and awe; from the root yod, resh, alef.

trapdoor: what you thought: fear of God means being scared of God.
what it means: yirah is fear and awe together: knowing how large the world is, and how small you are in it.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 28:17 pairs vayira and nora; Maimonides has love rise first, then awe, from contemplating creation.
